newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Nordic debt offers promise, pitfalls.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Nordic debt offers promise, pitfalls.

text.p: Nordic bonds could offer good value to global investors as European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) comes to the crunch, but these markets are not without their pitfalls, analysts said on Tuesday.
Analysts favoured Sweden or Denmark as the best earners thanks to sound economic fundamentals, but added that the former held political worries, while the latter held an inflation risk.
"Sweden and Denmark are stable markets with reasonable yield pick-ups in an environment where divergence pressures still exist in Europe," said Ifty Islam of Merrill Lynch in London.
Finland, analysts said, showed strong promise of qualifying for EMU convergence criteria, although this could prove a double edged sword as it had the most to lose from any delay.

Norway's fundamental attraction lay partly from the country's abundance of oil, which meant supply pressures were light because public finances were healthy, analysts said. But reliance on the volatile oil market was not the safest situation for investors, they added.
Analysts said they didn't believe Denmark, which holds an EMU opt-out clause, nor Sweden, which remains officially undecided, would participate in EMU from the outset.

"They're both interesting as opt-out markets in EMU," said Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill. "Both share good prospects for growth, but the market is still a little bit unclear as what the inflation implications of that will be."
"In Denmark and Sweden you get a yield pick-up on the core (EMU) countries...that would be the main attraction," said one Copenhagen-based analyst.
Swedish 10-year debt yields 110 basis points over benchmark German debt, while Danish bonds offer 67 basis points more.
In Sweden, recent data showed consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in December and were down 0.2 percent from a year before although analysts expected inflation to pick up this year.

Analysts said they feared the Swedish government would maintain its loose fiscal policies until after next year's general election, due to Prime Minister Goran Persson's dwindling support in opinion polls.
In Denmark, latest data showed inflation running at 2.6 percent in January. The government forecasts inflation of 2.3 percent in 1997.
The analyst in Copenhagen said although Danish growth figures were strong, there were no signs that it was rising.
"If Italy and Spain join from the outset, then investors might prefer to be in Denmark instead of being in the euro," the analyst added.
Merrill's Islam said that if you took EMU out of the equation, Sweden looked closer to reasonable valuations on the basis of domestic fundamentals than Italy or Spain.
Finnish bonds, on the other hand, would not benefit from any flows out from the core EMU members, analysts said.

"Finland stands a better chance of qualifying for EMU entry if it goes ahead, but...if there are any doubts about EMU going ahead investors stand to lose more in Finland than in the other markets," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.

James Mitchell, bond strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said Finland had a good chance of making it in the first wave, and said spreads against Bunds could come down from roughly 40 basis points to about 20 basis points.

One London-based trader said any time there was doubt about EMU he expected to see Finnish bonds lag. He said the market was very iliquid but hoped it would improve as investors realised it stood a fair chance of EMU entry.
Lewis said the Norwegian market reflected its dependence on oil and the worry was spreads would suffer as crude prices fell.

"While petrol was going up and we saw a situation where the 10-year spread relative to Germany came in from 70 basis points to zero...It's now going back out again because the oil price is well off its peak," he said.
But the Copenhagen analyst said Norwegian yields could dip below Germany given current economic conditions. They yielded a mere 10 basis points over Bunds on Tuesday.
